div.p: Inter-Task Energy-Hotspot Elimination in Fixed-Priority Real-Time Embedded Systems Mohsen Shekarisaz , Mehdi Kargahi , and Lothar Thiele , Life Member, IEEE Abstract-Multitask real-time embedded systems are often restricted by tight energy budgets, whilst they usually have environmental interactions through software-controlled energyhungry peripheral modules, such as LTE, WiFi, and GSM. The way that the driver calls are used within the embedded software to do such a control introduces program energy-hotspots (EHs) from the peripheral module perspective, namely, the code pieces wasting the system energy. By the energy waste, we mean that the energy consumption is reducible via some program code modifications without threatening the system schedulability and logical correctness. This article examines the program EHs of fixed-priority real-time tasks where two types of energy inefficiency can occur: 1) intra-task type, causing energy waste even if a task runs individually and 2) inter-task type, happening due to the interaction between different system tasks, namely, preemption scenarios even if there is no intra-task EH. The main cause of such EHs is the unnecessary time intervals between the driver calls, causing extra energy consumption by peripheral modules. We propose some static analysis methods to automatically detect and eliminate both types of intra-and inter-task EHs regarding their mutual relevance, according to the extreme (worst-case and best-case) execution times of certain task code parts. Our manipulations on the tasks to eliminate the EHs include some program code modifications with the awareness of system schedulability and logical correctness, and changing some scheduling decisions, namely, limiting the preemption points. After applying our proposed method to the test tasks, our simulation results show an energy reduction of up to 19%. Index Terms-Embedded software, embedded systems, energyhotspot (EH), peripheral modules, real-time scheduling.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: R EAL-TIME embedded systems, as major elements of cyber-physical systems (CPSs) and Internet of Things (IoT), usually come in the form of autonomous batteryoperated devices constituting of computational platforms, such as micro-controller units (MCUs) or microprocessors, augmented with energy-hungry peripheral modules (e.g., LTE, WiFi, and GSM). They run several real-time tasks (the software part) which work with such modules to provide various functionalities [1], however the inherent energy limitation of Mohsen Shekarisaz is with the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Tehran, Tehran 1439957131, Iran (e-mail: shekarisaz@ut.ac.ir).

Hence, in addition to the established requirements of logical correctness and system schedulability, a crucial design and implementation goal is to avoid wastage of energy when working with the modules. Dynamic power management (DPM) is a widely used runtime technique to deal with the steadily increasing [3] contribution of peripheral modules in energy consumption of such energy-limited real-time embedded systems. DPM approaches usually take care of the idle periods of the module in the Active state with respect to the state switching delay/energy overheads for switching to a Power-Saving state [4], [5]. However, after using the peripheral module through a driver call in the program code, and before such a switch, some energy may be wasted, known as tail energy [6], [7], [8], which may be as large as 60% of the module energy consumption [9]. Some design-time static power management decisions, especially in the software program level [10], may help reducing such an energy wastage; for example, appropriate placement of the driver calls of peripheral modules among MCU computational instructions in the program code of real-time tasks is of this type, which can affect the length of idle periods, and thus, the corresponding power state switches. An example is depicted in Fig. 1(a), showing that two close driver calls can avoid the extra tail energy belonging to the first one. If some module energy wastage could be avoided through program code modification with respect to the driver calls without threatening the software logical and temporal correctness, as well as without any negative impact on the energy consumption under any running scenario, we name the wastage a program energy-hotspot (EH) [11], [12]. Detection and elimination of such EHs in a single-task system has been studied in [12]; this article studies the problem in multitasking systems, since the interaction between different system tasks reveals some previously unnoticed energy problems.

While it may not be possible to implement programs without EHs in a general sense, we can focus on addressing specific program EHs with significant impacts on system energy consumption through two main types of EHs: 1) intra-task and 2) inter-task. The former is an issue within a task, which wastes energy even if the program code of the task runs individually. The latter, however, only is raised in a multitask system, due to the interaction between the tasks via the real-time scheduler decisions, namely, the preemption time. An inter-task EH may result in energy wastage even if the individual task program codes have no intra-task EH. Fig. 1(b) shows an example that either executing MCU instructions of the same task between the driver calls, or preemption by a higher priority task shortly after the completion of the first driver call of the former task results in the extra tail energy; although the latter is a problem that only occurs in a multitasking system.

We can use a limited-preemption approach [13], [14] to deal with inter-task EHs. However, as we will discuss, this cannot be done in isolation from the elimination of EHs within tasks, i.e., a co-design approach is required. More precisely, the size of non-preemptive program segments may affect the system schedulability [15]. The size can be decreased by the driver call movements regarding the intra-task EHs of different tasks; to take care of the schedulability impacts.

This article studies program EH detection and elimination of multitask fixed-priority real-time embedded systems using static analysis methods, regarding both inter-task and intratask EHs, exploiting the worst-case execution time (WCET) and best-case execution time (BCET) of specific program code pieces of the tasks.

We evaluate our approach through extensive simulations on diverse test task sets from the TACLeBench [16] benchmark suite, augmented with driver calls injected in the benchmark programs on the basis of real embedded programs. Upon comparing the energy consumption of the original and manipulated tasks of different task sets, we observe energy reduction of up to 19%, described in detail in the corresponding section. In summary, the contributions of this article are as follows.

1) Introducing the type of inter-task EH in multitasking real-time embedded systems, as a complement to the already defined intra-task type [12] in single-task systems. 2) Proposing some static code analysis methods (i.e., with no need to program execution) for the EH detection. 3) Providing some algorithms for simultaneous consideration of the identified intra-task and inter-task EHs, and deciding about the way of EH elimination by modifying the task program codes in accordance to a limited preemption approach, whilst preserving the system schedulability and the tasks logical correctness. We prove that, in a hyperperiod, our manipulations do not cause any running scenario to consume some extra amount of energy when compared to the system before the manipulations, namely, we show that our proposed method is safe with respect to energy wastage. 4) The inclusion of comprehensive simulation results for different test task sets, to showcase the effectiveness of our approach in reducing the system energy consumption through avoiding some specific sort of energy wastage. The remainder of this article is organized as follows. We discuss the related works in Section II. We give our system model in Section III. In Sections IV and V, respectively, we provide the formal definition of EHs and the problem statement. Section VII provides some requisites and the algorithms for EH detection and elimination. In Section VII, we discuss the simulation results, illustrating the efficacy of the proposed method. Finally, Section VIII concludes and offers insights for further research.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: This section reviews the related studies from perspectives of program EH, peripheral module energy consumption, and limited preemption, taking care of approaches at different levels of task program code, scheduler, and system.

Program EHs: There exist both dynamic and static analysis methods for the problem of program EH detection. Dynamic analysis approaches [11], [17], as opposed to static analysis, reveal EHs at the expense of program execution and runtime energy measurements. On the side of static analysis, Banerjee et al. [18] concentrated on program energy bugs, i.e., when a peripheral module continues to consume energy even after completion of the program execution. In [12] and [19], however, some specific intra-task EHs, respectively, in the contexts of single-task real-time and non-real-time embedded systems have been studied. Nonetheless, none of these methods consider EHs in multitask systems, causing inter-task EHs. This article simultaneously considers both intra-and inter-task EHs in real-time embedded systems, and provides some algorithms to detect and eliminate them, preserving the system logical and temporal correctness.

Energy Consumption of Peripheral Modules: Regarding the energy consumption of peripheral modules, DPM stands out as one of the most promising techniques. The main idea is to switch the module to a lower power state to unneeded energy consumption, usually on the basis of timeout or prediction policies [4], [5]. The hardware-based approaches need an extra hardware component for managing power states [20], while the software-based approaches are usually implemented at the OS- [21], compiler- [22] or device-driver-level [23]. Some module energy issues like tail energy [6], [7], [8], however, cannot be addressed by DPM, because the way that a task program uses the module via driver calls greatly impacts the module energy consumption. Thus, this article focuses on the program level.

Evaluating the module energy consumption at the program code level has been the subject of some studies. For instance, [3] and [24] proposed measurement-based methods for generating automata-based power model of peripheral modules in embedded systems automatically based on energy measurements. Furthermore, energy profiling of peripheral modules has been investigated in [25]. The main objective of such module energy evaluation techniques, however, is to provide valuable knowledge about the energy consumed by driver calls, to be used in cycle-accurate simulation of the system; thus, the empowered developers can be aware of the energy consumption of their programs during development. Nonetheless, the studies lack emphasis on leveraging driver calls for energy improvement.

CPU/MCU Energy Reduction: Some previous studies focus on energy reduction of embedded devices through other techniques such as limited preemption scheduling, which has been exploited as a hybrid technique to take advantage of both types of fully-and non-preemptive scheduling models. For instance, Bambagini et al. [26] proposed an online DPM technique for prolonging sleep intervals, while it exploits a limited preemption approach under fixed-priority systems. Bambagini et al. [27] investigated the potential impacts that preemption overheads might have on the energy consumption. Moreover, a number of previous works in the literature deal with reducing CPU energy consumption through dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), with the awareness of peak power consumption [28], tasks quality of service [29], and circuit-level aging effect [30]. However, these studies focus on CPU/MCU energy consumption, and they do not address the energy wastage of peripheral modules in relation to the driver calls. Furthermore, in peripheral modules that make environmental interactions, using voltage/frequency scaling is not usually applicable due to hardware constraints, performance requirements, and potential compatibility issues.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this section, we present the hardware model, software model, and the embedded software energy model, while Table I tabulates their nomenclature that we explain in the following.

div.head: A. Hardware Model
div.p: The target hardware platform consists of a micro-controllerbased computational unit, denoted as MCU, and a set of peripheral modules (resources), shown as R = {r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n }.

According to the related studies on energy modeling [3], [7], a wide variety of peripheral modules, such as network transceivers and sensors (as examples of r i ) provide a set of power states. Inspired by them, Fig. 2 illustrates an abstract state model of a typical module r i , described by a continuous timed automata (X represents the clock), along with the delay and power consumption corresponding to the states.

Each r i is acquired (i.e., powered on) whenever it is registered by a software task, and it is released (i.e., powered off) when the task terminates; in other words, r i remains acquired during the task lifetime, however, it may be put in different power states in between. As it can be seen in Fig. 2, the acquired module is initially ready for use in the Active state. Each r i has a built-in DPM unit (see [31]) to avoid energy wastage happening due to unnecessarily being idle in Active; it puts the module into a lower power state, namely, Power-Saving, after a (possibly configurable) timeout of being idle in Active,1 i.e., D A (r i ).

A driver call, modeled as a single statement of Use(r i , d), is executed by the embedded software to manipulate the state of r i . By executing Use(r i , d) when r i is in Active or Power-Saving r i is put into the Use state to perform some operations on data d; it takes a delay of D U (r i ) to complete the operation,2 with a power usage of P U (r i ). The energy consumption to perform the operation is E U (r i ) = D U (r i )P U (r i ). After passing D U (r i ), r i starts to return back to Active, with a power usage of P T (r i ), and taking a delay of D T (r i ) to complete the transition. However, if another Use(r i , d) is called in between, r i does not complete the transition to Active; rather, it returns to Use and starts to perform as described above.

Suppose t = 0 is the time when the kth Use(r i , d) is finished. We show the time interval from t = 0 to the next call of Use(r i , d) as I i,k (I i,0 is the interval from acquiring r i until the call of the first Use(r i , d) statement). Therefore, after finishing the kth Use(r i , d), r i consumes some tail energy E T (r i , I i,k ) as follows:

Additionally, during the interval I i,k , r i may spend some time in Active and Power-Saving; thus, depending on the sojourn time in each state and the corresponding power consumption P A (r i ) and P S (r i ), it consumes there some energy E A (r i , I i,k ) and E S (r i , I i,k ), respectively.

Regarding MCU, it can run either computational instructions or module-related statements [i.e., Use(r i , d)], causing two MCU states: 1) Busy (with power consumption of P B ), in which it executes a computational instruction and 2) Idle (with power consumption of P I ), in which either there is no computational instruction to be run on MCU (lack of workload) or it waits for r i to respond. Despite [19] which has studied the non-blocking model of driver calls, without loss of generality, in this article we assume that MCU spends a delay D U (r i ) in the Idle state for every Use(r i , d) statement.

div.head: IV. ENERGY HOTSPOTS
div.p: This section gives a general definition for program EH, makes it specific to Use(r i , d), and categorizes it under intratask and inter-task EHs in multitask real-time systems. A motivating example is also provided.

div.head: A. Definitions and Categories
div.p: From the driver call perspective, a task program code is free of EHs, if the module used by the task wastes no energy; more precisely, it is EH-free, if the driver calls have located at right places in the program code such that there is no better place to have a holistic (i.e., for all program paths) energy improvement without violating time constraints or logical correctness.

In multitask environments, EHs can be categorized as two types of intra-task and inter-task, which the former relates to the direct places of driver calls within a task program code; and the latter is defined based on the interaction between the tasks of different priorities through preemption policies, which can dynamically affect the relative places of the driver calls. Thus, elimination of intra-task EHs is done via program code modification, i.e., by moving the driver calls back/forth in there; and elimination of inter-task EHs is done through the preemption policies, i.e., by performing the preemptions aware of the driver call places of different tasks, possibly via some dynamic hints from the program code. In this article, we take care of both intra-and inter-task EHs with respect to the Use(r i , d) driver calls with regard to tail energy [6], [7], [8], namely, a well-known energy issue with a contribution up to 60% of the total module energy consumption [9].

1) Intra-Task Tail EH: An intra-task Tail EH of r i (related to τ i ) is defined based on the time distance between successive Use(r i , d) statements in the corresponding program paths, i.e., I i,k of the kth Use(r i , d) statement in each path of the program. Since

If we could manipulate the program code of τ i by placing the kth Use(r i , d) statement just beside (k + 1)th Use(r i , d) statement in the same program path (or place the latter just after the former), then we would have I i,k = 0 and E T (I i,k ) = 0, namely, the intra-task EH could be eliminated. However, this is not necessarily feasible because of the dependencies between the statements, reflected in MPDG i .

div.head: V. PROBLEM DEFINITION
div.p: The task set energy optimization in the general form is an intractable problem. Thus, some heuristics toward eliminating the detected EHs may be provided to guarantee that the energy is reduced. In the context of single-task real-time embedded systems, such a problem for intra-task EHs has been studied in [12]. In this article, thus we focus on multitask systems, where inter-task EHs may arise along with the intra-task type.
Aiming to eliminate the intra-and inter-task EHs, we define a set of manipulation actions.

1) The program modification action is to modify the program code of each task τ i ∈ τ , say converting it to τ i , which comprises moving the Use nodes of MCFG i forward or backward, and replicating/merging them whenever needed.

2) The limited preemption action is to find a set of energy-ineffective PPs (EIPPs) ρ i ⊆ E MCFG i for τ i ∈ τ , in order to prevent the possible preemptions at these points; namely, enforcing some module-related paths in program code of τ i (i.e., paths between consecutive Use nodes in MCFG i ) to run non-preemptively. Objective: Suppose a given real-time task set τ of an embedded system according to the model of Section III, which is logically correct and schedulable according to a given fixed priority order. The goal is to detect intra-and intertask EHs of the tasks in τ , and manipulate them by the above-mentioned manipulation actions, toward EH elimination, preserving the task set logical correctness and schedulability. More specifically, each manipulation should be performed in such a way that ensures it does not have any adverse effect on the system energy consumption, and on the task set logical correctness and schedulability. Consequently, we construct the modified tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , and correspondingly the set of EIPPs ρ 1 , ρ 2 , . . . , ρ n , such that the energy consumption of τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } in a hyperperiod H of every possible interleaving of the task runs (an individual program path is taken at each task run) gets better than (or remains the same as) that of τ for the same runs, namely Energy τ , H ≤ Energy(τ, H).

div.head: VI. DETECTION AND ELIMINATION
div.p: Suppose we have a task set τ , along with the energy and time specifications of the set of modules (resources) R, according to the model of Section III. We provide some static code analysis method which traverses MCFG i of each task τ i top-down toward intra-task and inter-task EH detection; and acts some manipulations for their elimination. The topdown approach means that the EHs related to a Use node n i,j are detected and eliminated after doing the same actions for prev Use (n i,j ), and before doing so for next Use (n i,j ). The result will then be a task set τ of modified program codes of the tasks, each with a set of EIPPs ρ i , consistent to the system schedulability and the dependencies reflected in MPDG i of τ i . Since we study a static analysis approach, we do not make any assumptions or rely on any information regarding the runtime behavior of the tasks with respect to execution frequency of the individual program paths, namely, whether a path is executed rarely or frequently. Thus, we act our manipulations on τ i based on extreme scenarios, namely, partial BCETs/WCETs of specific program pieces, targeting the property that the energy consumption of all program paths under all runtime behaviors should get better than (or remain the same as) those of the original task set.

The non-preemptive regions in the program code of a task may defer some preemptions, i.e., the preemption times are moved and the original schedule thus may be changed. On the other hand, according to Corollary 2, we should ensure that a preemption in a manipulated task does not have any adverse energy impact in comparison to the original system. Due to the variation of the program execution paths and correspondingly the task execution times, the time/place of a preemption is not known a priori [15]; thus, our strategy is to protect all pieces of the program codes with the potential of energy wastage due to preemptions. More precisely, the beneficial effect of energy through eliminating an inter-task EH in τ i cannot be ensured without protecting the paths between any two Use nodes of MCFG j for each τ j ∈ τ , whose execution time is less than D T (r j ); otherwise, there is no guarantee that a non-preemptive path between two Use nodes of MCFG i does not have adverse impact on the energy, compared to the original task schedule. div.head: B. Detection and Elimination Algorithms
div.p: Our main algorithm, called detection and elimination of intra-and inter-task EHs (DIMINISH), is presented in Algorithm 1. Given a task set τ , DIMINISH eliminates the intra-and inter-task EHs, and returns a task set τ (of modified program codes) and a set of EIPPs ρ. Our proposed static analysis method can be used in practice by integrating the DIMINISH functionality into the middle-end or back-end workflows of the compiler.

Computational Complexity: To clarify the scalability aspect, we discuss our proposed method in terms of significant complexity factors related to the contribution of this article. DIMINISH detects and eliminates the EHs of each task separately, resulting in a linear relationship of computational complexity with the number of tasks, i.e., n. For each task τ i , provisioning of MCFG i and MPDG i linearly depends on the program code size, specifically on the instruction count. Since compilers typically require these graphs for different analyses they are constructed; further, the BFS traversal of MCFG i to visit the Use nodes imposes linear complexity concerning N MCFG i + E MCFG i (i.e., the nodes and edges of MCFG i ), which is usually done by the compiler during other types of analysis (e.g., data-flow analysis). Meanwhile, the number of Use nodes related to peripheral module r i , i.e., Num U (r i ), necessitates additional BFS traversals within the related partial MCFG i for calculations and the rule checking purposes, which we consider the worst-case scenario of full traversal of MCFG i per Use node. Moreover, manipulations toward EH elimination (node movements and non-preemptive enforcements) do not impose significant complexity. Thus, DIMINISH scalability is mainly connected to the number of Use nodes and the corresponding program size, namely, it exhibits a complex-

div.head: VII. EVALUATION
div.p: This section provides extensive simulation results to show the efficacy of the proposed method in comparison to some approaches, and provides some complementary discussions. Given our emphasis on the schedulability of the original and manipulated task sets, the focus of our evaluations is on the energy consumption aspect of the system.

div.head: A. Simulation Setup
div.p: We setup our simulations by employing a set of tools, hardware datasheets, and benchmark applications, because the energy-aware simulators of embedded devices (like MEET [36]) do not fully accommodate the entire system, i.e., to simultaneously include peripheral modules and energy models, PPs, and task codes; as we need in this study.

System Configuration: We consider the embedded hardware as an AT91SAM7X256 MCU with an ARM7TDMI processor and 64 kB of SRAM, equipped with a set of peripheral modules, including LTE BG96 [37], WiFi ESP8266 [38], RF Transceiver CC2420 [39], Bluetooth HC-05 [40], GSM SIM900 [41], and Flash AT25SF161 [42]; which have significant contribution in deploying embedded systems of the market [43]. We use MEET to simulate the energy consumption and the execution times of the computational instructions. The time, energy, and power specifications of the modules have been extracted from the datasheets. We combine the time and energy of the computational instructions and those of the driver calls of equipped peripheral modules together, to simulate the behavior of the whole system.

Multitask Applications (Task Sets): The multitask applications used for the evaluations are composed of sets of 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 periodic tasks, denoted, respectively, by APP 1, APP 2, APP 3, APP 4, and APP 5, tabulated in Table III. As multitask applications in most embedded devices involve various tasks that perform the well-known operations of receiving, processing, and transmitting data, the program code of tasks should comprise both computational parts and module-related statements. We selected the computational parts from TACLeBench benchmark suite [16], as a set of open-source embedded programs without any dependencies on standard libraries and operating systems. The selection encompasses various application types in the realm of embedded devices. Then, we augment the computational parts of each task with module-related statements, as described below. Augmentation Setups: For a task τ i , the module r i is randomly selected from the modules in the system configuration. To augment Use(r i , d) statements (i.e., Use nodes) in the task program code, we afford four Augmentation SetUps of ASU 1, ASU 2, ASU 3, and ASU 4, shown in Table IV. The parameters of an augmentation setup are the minimum and maximum ratios of Use nodes to Comp nodes in a given program execution path, and they are set to encompass a spectrum of sparse to dense Use nodes among Comp nodes. Also, the placement of Use nodes in the augmentations is inspired from some real embedded programs in [44]. More specifically, we select a set of six open-source programs of module-equipped embedded systems with respect to the modules in the system configuration; and in each program, we obtain the distributions of Use(r i , d) statements for more than 15 program execution paths. By distribution, we mean the probability of having a Use(r i , d) statement in distinct parts of a program path (i.e., dispersion among computational instructions). Then, we augment specific paths of each task program code of Table III according to some randomly selected distribution among them. This way, Use(r i , d) statements in the task program are called in a pattern that aligns with the real-world counterparts. Although experimenting on real-world applications may show other evaluation aspects, we consider it as a direction for our further studies.

Analyzer: We used SWEET [45] as our program analysis tool to extract the CFG/PDG, find program execution paths, and calculate the (partial) BCETs/WCETs. Further, the partial graphs are converted to distinct functions in order to calculate the needed partial BCETs/WCETs.

Tasks Time/Priority Properties: We vary the system total utilization to be in the range of [0.1, 0.9] with the stride of 0.1. The utilization of each task, namely, (C i /T i ), is assigned randomly according to the UUnifast algorithm [46] to satisfy the given total utilization. Furthermore, we calculated C i by SWEET, which corresponds to the program path with the highest execution time in the program code of τ i . Thus, the time properties including T i as well as Q i are obtained. Finally, the rate monotonic algorithm is chosen to assign fixed priorities, given its widespread usage in the field of real-time systems, where a lower T i indicates a higher priority.

Applied Methods: We apply three methods on the original applications (i.e., with no manipulations), and compare the results. The methods include: 1) DIMINISH, i.e., our proposed method to eliminate intra-and inter-task EHs through scheduler-aware program modifications; 2) EHDE [19], which is a method only concerning intra-task EHs through program modifications; and 3) the longest non-preemptive budget [15], referred to as LNPB, which greedily exploits the nonpreemptive budget for module-related program pieces to avoid inter-task EHs, however without any program modification.

Simulation Platform: The analyses and simulations were performed on an Intel CoreTM i7-4720HQ processor and 16 GB of RAM. Table III illustrates the instruction counts normalized to APP 5, showing a relative approximation of the amount of computational parts of applications, and the average offline static analysis times of applying DIMINISH.

div.head: B. Simulation Results
div.p: The simulation results are obtained from 20 multitask test applications, which are constituted as APP 1 to APP 5 under ASU 1 to ASU 4. The program code of a task τ i may take distinct running paths based on the task inputs. According to the input data set of the benchmark package, we randomly select some program paths (including the one corresponding to C i ), augment them in accordance to the corresponding ASU, and take them as the task runs in a hyperperiod, so that the simulation energy consumption resembles that of a realworld system. Further, for each test application, we perform the simulations per different total utilization value, and then average the results. Fig. 5 reports the total energy improvements as well as the separated cases for the modules states, resulted from applying DIMINISH, EHDE, and LNPB, with respect to the original test applications. Several aspects, namely the temporal and dependency restrictions, the augmentation setups (i.e., the number and distribution of Use nodes as well as the preemption requests), and the number and execution times of Comp nodes in the programs, affect the energy improvements, which we will discuss further. The best-case improvement, with 11.01% total energy reduction, relates to APP 5 in ASU 4; and the worst-case improvement, with 2.93% total energy reduction, relates to APP 1 in ASU 1.

Since DIMINISH eliminates both types of intra-and intertask EHs, the modules tail energy is reduced by 19.7% on average, i.e., more than EHDE (by 9.66% on average) and LNPB (by 4.42% on average) which only concern intra-task and inter-task EHs, respectively. Furthermore, bringing the Use nodes together by applying DIMINISH makes the DPM policy of the module more effective because continuous idle times of the module are increased; thus, the time being in Active is also improved, and the module stays longer in Power-Saving; that the energy of this state is increased. Note that LNPB has had the least amount of improvement in most cases.

1) Regarding the greedy approach in protecting modulerelated pieces of programs without any modification, the non-preemptive budget is not efficiently exploited, so that LNPB cannot protect all intended pieces due to the schedulability violation. 2) Due to such unprotected pieces, LNPB fails to comply with energy-safe limited preemption (Rule 4), which may cause additional unpredictable tail energy consumption. Fig. 6 illustrates the distribution of interval I i,k , as well as the contribution of task execution and preemption in the consumed tail energy in different methods (normalized to the original test applications), averaged over different test applications. Regarding D T (r i ), Use nodes that are close to each other (time intervals of zero and closer to zero) contribute more when DIMINISH is applied, unlike the contribution of Use nodes that are far apart (time intervals close to D T (r i ) or even more).

EHDE works better than DIMINISH in terms of tail energy due to execution since it does not care about schedulability, rather it more freely eliminates the intra-task EHs. However, DIMINISH smooths inter-task EHs elimination, and in total it causes further tail energy improvement, even though tail energy due to preemption (with 15%) has had on the average a lesser effect than tail energy due to execution (with 85%) in the original applications. Nonetheless, the replacement of some Use nodes in EHDE with no non-preemptive enforcement may cause some tail energy due to preemption with respect to close Use nodes, and thus, the contribution increases compared to the original applications. Note that the contribution of preemption in tail energy is not zero by DIMINISH; the reason is the impossibility of manipulating some task sets due to the schedulability violation (see Rule 4). Fig. 7 depicts more details on the reduced energy and the contributions of the EH types when DIMINISH is applied. By the increase of programs sizes from APP 1 to APP 5, the time distances between the consecutive Use nodes in a task program code increase as well; therefore, the probability that a preemption causes an inter-task EH is lowered (since D T (r i ) is probably passed), although it directly increases the chance of eliminating more intra-task EHs. However, when the density (and subsequently, the number) of Use nodes increases from ASU 1 to ASU 4, the time distances between the consecutive Use nodes may decrease; thus, a preemption leads to an inter-task EH with higher probability, although these shorter distances cause less chance to reduce the energy through the elimination of intra-task EHs. Accordingly, the best-case contribution of inter-task EHs refers to APP 1 with ASU 4 (about 48%), and the worst-case contribution refers to APP 5 with ASU 1 (about 8%). Note that, as a method that only eliminates inter-task EHs, LNPB has its best and worst performances in similar situations (see Fig. 5).

Due to the long execution time of high-priority tasks (compared to D T (r i ) of a module), the maximum fixed value of tail energy [i.e., E T (r i , D T (r i ))] is usually imposed by a preemption between two adjacent Use nodes of a low priority task. However, on the average, the contribution of inter-task EHs (about 33%) is less than intra-task type (about 67%); the root cause is that a preemption happening exactly between two adjacent Use nodes is less likely compared to the fixed time distances between them within a program, at least in our test applications (see Fig. 6).

Finally, we investigate the total utilization effect on energy reduction by DIMINISH, shown in Fig. 8, where the results are reported as an average over different applications. Since the total utilization in a fixed priority system may affect the number of preemptions (especially for the high values of utilization) [15], with the increase of utilization, the chance of a preemption being placed between two adjacent Use nodes directly increases, and the probability of tail energy wastage rises up; thus, given an augmentation setup, DIMINISH performs more effectively by eliminating more inter-task EHs. Moreover, when the density of Use nodes grows up (i.e., from ASU 1 to ASU 4), nodes become closer to and therefore, a preemption is more likely to waste some tail energy. Furthermore, on higher utilization values where the number of preemptions increases remarkably, the energy improvement is more significant for higher densities. Overall, we see the best-case total energy reduction of 19%.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: Energy consumption, as a non-functional aspect, is a significant concern in energy-limited real-time embedded devices which are designed to provide a wide range of applications, especially in multitask systems. Software programs of embedded tasks have an important role on the consumed energy since they instruct the hardware components to perform the desired operations. This article addresses intra-and inter-task program EHs related to the peripheral modules, and proposes some schedulability-aware program modification via a limited preemption policy to eliminate the EHs; with no adverse effect on the logical correctness and the energy consumption of the system. Our simulation results show about 19% of energy reduction, providing evidence to support the effectiveness of the proposed method. As of future work, we aim to broaden the scope of our method to encompass beyond fixedpriority scheduling strategies. Also, we plan to extend our research to a wider range of EHs regarding energy issues of more sophisticated modules-equipped embedded devices, and implement our approach as a comprehensive framework.
